\section[saṁsārikkuka]{\ml{സംസാരിക്കുക} (saṁsārikkuka) — \textquotedblleft{}to speak,\textquotedblright{} your first full verb}

\label{lesson:ML-C05-samsaarikkuka}



\begin{quote}
So far, \textquotedblleft{}to be.\textquotedblright{} Here is a verb that \emph{does} something — and it reveals the single strangest, simplest thing about Malayalam grammar.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{സം}} (\emph{saṁ}) + \textbf{\ml{സാ}} (\emph{sā}) + \textbf{\ml{രി}} (\emph{ri}) + \textbf{\ml{ക്കുക}} (\emph{kkuka}, doubled \emph{kk} + the \emph{-uka} infinitive) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{സംസാരിക്കുക}} (\emph{saṁsārikkuka}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{സംസാരിക്കുക}} (\emph{saṁsārikkuka}, \textquotedblleft{}to speak, to converse\textquotedblright{}) is Sanskrit-derived (from \emph{saṃsāra}, \textquotedblleft{}flowing together, intercourse\textquotedblright{}) — one more sign of Malayalam's deep Sanskrit layer, alongside its native \emph{paṟayuka} (\textquotedblleft{}to say\textquotedblright{}). To say \textquotedblleft{}I speak,\textquotedblright{} Malayalam adds the present ending \textbf{-\ml{ഉന്നു}} (\emph{-unnu}) to the stem:

\begin{quote}
\emph{saṁsārikk-} (speak) + \emph{-unnu} (present) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{സംസാരിക്കുന്നു}} (\emph{saṁsārikkunnu}), \textquotedblleft{}speak / am speaking.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the verb never changes for person}]
Here is Malayalam's great surprise. In Tamil, Telugu, and Kannada the verb changes ending for \emph{who} acts (\emph{pēsugiṟēṉ} \textquotedblleft{}I speak,\textquotedblright{} \emph{pēsugiṟāṉ} \textquotedblleft{}he speaks\textquotedblright{}). \textbf{Malayalam does not.} The verb is the \textbf{same} for everyone:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ñān saṁsārikkunnu} — \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{nī saṁsārikkunnu} — \textquotedblleft{}you speak\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{avan saṁsārikkunnu} — \textquotedblleft{}he speaks\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

One form, all persons. Malayalam threw away person-agreement entirely — which is exactly why (Chapter 3) it can never drop the pronoun: the verb won't tell you who. Of all its Dravidian sisters, Malayalam went the furthest here.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}saṁsārikkuka\textquotedblright{} (to speak)
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ñān saṁsārikkunnu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}he speaks\textquotedblright{} — \emph{avan saṁsārikkunnu} (the same verb!)
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{pōkuka}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does the Malayalam verb change between \textquotedblleft{}I speak\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}he speaks,\textquotedblright{} and what does that force you to keep? (It does \textbf{not} change — one form for all persons; so the pronoun must always be said.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ña]{\ml{ഞ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S115-letter-nya}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{◌ൂ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has been sitting in front of you on pages you have already read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{ഞ}}
\textbf{\ml{ഞ}} — \emph{ña}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ñ}, it is \textbf{ña}.

You have said the word for \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} since the how-are-you chapter, and it starts with this letter.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} \emph{ñān} — I
\end{itemize}

It is one sound, not two: the \emph{ny} of \textquotedblleft{}canyon,\textquotedblright{} made in one movement.

\section[n]{\ml{ൻ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S142-chillu-n}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ഞ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has been sitting in front of you on pages you have already read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{ൻ}}
\textbf{\ml{ൻ}} — \emph{n}.

It is a \textbf{chillu} — a consonant with its vowel stripped away and given a shape of its own, so that it can end a word without a dangling mark.

The same word ends with a chillu — the third one you have met.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} \emph{ñān} — I
  \item \textbf{\ml{നിങ്ങൾ}} \emph{niṅṅaḷ} — you, respectful, ending in \textbf{\ml{ൾ}}
  \item \textbf{\ml{അരുൺ}} \emph{aruṇ} — the name, ending in \textbf{\ml{ൺ}}
\end{itemize}

\textbf{\ml{ൻ}} is \textbf{\ml{ന}} with its \emph{a} handed back. Line the three up — \textbf{\ml{ൻ} \ml{ൺ} \ml{ൾ}} — and say what each one used to be.

\section[ñān malayāḷaṁ saṁsārikkunnu]{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{സംസാരിക്കുന്നു} (ñān malayāḷaṁ saṁsārikkunnu) — \textquotedblleft{}I speak Malayalam\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C05-njaan-malayalam-samsaarikkunnu}



\begin{quote}
Your first full, moving sentence — and the language names itself after a landscape.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{മലയാളം}} (\emph{malayāḷaṁ}): \textbf{\ml{മ}} (\emph{ma}) + \textbf{\ml{ല}} (\emph{la}) + \textbf{\ml{യാ}} (\emph{yā}) + \textbf{\ml{ള}} (retroflex \emph{ḷa}) + \textbf{\ml{ം}} (\emph{ṁ}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{മലയാളം} \ml{സംസാരിക്കുന്നു}} = \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} (\emph{ñān}, \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ml{മലയാളം}} (\emph{malayāḷaṁ}, the object) + \textbf{\ml{സംസാരിക്കുന്നു}} (\emph{saṁsārikkunnu}, \textquotedblleft{}speak\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}I Malayalam speak,\textquotedblright{} the verb last. The name \textbf{\ml{മലയാളം}} (\emph{malayāḷaṁ}) is native Dravidian: \textbf{\ml{മല}} (\emph{mala}, \textquotedblleft{}mountain\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ml{ആളം}} (\emph{āḷaṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}place, region\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{the mountain land},\textquotedblright{} named for the Western Ghats along the coast where it is spoken. Its signature retroflex \textbf{\ml{ള}} (\emph{ḷ}) sits right in the middle of the word.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the pronoun stays}]
Because \emph{saṁsārikkunnu} is the same for every person (Chapter 5's big surprise), the pronoun \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} (\emph{ñān}) cannot be dropped — it is the only thing marking \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I}.\textquotedblright{} Where Tamil would happily say just \emph{pēsugiṟēṉ}, Malayalam must keep the \emph{ñān}.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ñān malayāḷaṁ saṁsārikkunnu\textquotedblright{}
  \item what \emph{malayāḷaṁ} is built from (\emph{mala} \textquotedblleft{}mountain\textquotedblright{} + \emph{āḷaṁ} \textquotedblleft{}place\textquotedblright{})
  \item why \emph{ñān} can't be dropped (the verb doesn't mark person)
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}I speak Malayalam,\textquotedblright{} and give the meaning of the language's name. (\emph{Ñān malayāḷaṁ saṁsārikkunnu}; \textquotedblleft{}the mountain land,\textquotedblright{} \emph{mala} + \emph{āḷaṁ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o]{\ml{◌ൊ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S143-vowel-sign-o}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{യ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has not been on a page yet: it arrives with the word on the next one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{◌ൊ}}
\textbf{\ml{◌ൊ}} — \emph{o}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{o}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{കൊച്ചി}} \emph{kocci} — Kochi, the city that arrives on the next page
\end{itemize}

It is the short partner of \textbf{\ml{◌ോ}}, the long \emph{ō} sign you copied in \textbf{\ml{സന്തോഷം}}. Both wrap around their consonant, one arm in front and one behind; the long one carries an extra upright stroke on the right.

Put your pen on \ml{◌ൊ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

\section[l]{\ml{ൽ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S144-chillu-l}

It is a \textbf{chillu} — a consonant with its vowel stripped away and given a shape of its own, so that it can end a word without a dangling mark.

\section[tāmasikkuka]{\ml{താമസിക്കുക} (tāmasikkuka) — \textquotedblleft{}to live, to stay\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C05-taamasikkuka}



\begin{quote}
A second verb, so you can say where you live — and again the Sanskrit layer shows.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{താ}} (\emph{tā}) + \textbf{\ml{മ}} (\emph{ma}) + \textbf{\ml{സി}} (\emph{si}) + \textbf{\ml{ക്കുക}} (\emph{kkuka}, the \emph{-uka} infinitive) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{താമസിക്കുക}} (\emph{tāmasikkuka}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{താമസിക്കുക}} (\emph{tāmasikkuka}, \textquotedblleft{}to live, to reside, to stay, to delay\textquotedblright{}) is Sanskrit-derived (from \emph{tāmasa} / \emph{tamas}, \textquotedblleft{}dwelling, tarrying\textquotedblright{}). Malayalam often prefers such Sanskrit-built verbs where Tamil uses a native word (\emph{vāḻ}). \textquotedblleft{}I live in Kochi\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{കൊച്ചിയിൽ} \ml{താമസിക്കുന്നു}} (\emph{ñān kocciyil tāmasikkunnu}) — again the same \emph{-unnu} present, the same for every person.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} comes after the noun}]
\textbf{\ml{കൊച്ചിയിൽ}} (\emph{kocciyil}) = \emph{Kochi} + \textbf{-\ml{ഇൽ}} (\emph{-il}, \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{}), glued to the \textbf{end} of the noun. Malayalam uses \textbf{post}positions (case-suffixes) where English uses prepositions: \textquotedblleft{}Kochi-in I live,\textquotedblright{} the verb last — and the pronoun kept.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}tāmasikkuka\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I live in Kochi\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ñān kocciyil tāmasikkunnu}
  \item where \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} (\emph{-il}) sits — glued to the end of the noun
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{tāmasikkuka} mean, and where does \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} go? (\textquotedblleft{}To live / stay / reside\textquotedblright{}; \emph{-il} \textquotedblleft{}in\textquotedblright{} attaches to the \textbf{end} of the noun.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[jōli ceyyuka]{\ml{ജോലി} \ml{ചെയ്യുക} (jōli ceyyuka) — \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C05-joli-ceyyuka}



\begin{quote}
The last verb of the chapter — and, like Hindi's \emph{karnā} and Tamil's \emph{sey}, it is a \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{} verb that builds a hundred others.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{ജോലി}} (\emph{jōli}, \textquotedblleft{}work, job\textquotedblright{}): \textbf{\ml{ജോ}} (\emph{jō}) + \textbf{\ml{ലി}} (\emph{li}). \textbf{\ml{ചെയ്യുക}} (\emph{ceyyuka}, \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{}): \textbf{\ml{ചെ}} (\emph{ce}) + \textbf{\ml{യ്യു}} (doubled \emph{yy}) + \textbf{\ml{ക}} (\emph{ka}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{ചെയ്യുക}} (\emph{ceyyuka}, \textquotedblleft{}to do, to make\textquotedblright{}) is core native Dravidian — the very same root as Tamil \textbf{\ta{செய்}} (\emph{sey}, \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{}). Malayalam — like Hindi with \emph{karnā}, Tamil with \emph{sey}, Telugu with \emph{cēyu}, Kannada with \emph{māḍu} — builds compound verbs by putting a noun in front of it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ജോലി} \ml{ചെയ്യുക}} (\emph{jōli ceyyuka}) = \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{} = \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{to work}\textquotedblright{} (\emph{jōli}, \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textbf{\ml{സഹായിക്കുക}} (\emph{sahāyikkuka}) = \textquotedblleft{}to help\textquotedblright{} (Sanskrit \emph{sahāya})
\end{itemize}

So \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} is \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{ജോലി} \ml{ചെയ്യുന്നു}} (\emph{ñān jōli ceyyunnu}) — same \emph{-unnu} present, pronoun kept. \emph{Ceyyuka} and Tamil's \emph{sey} are, at root, one word — the Dravidian \textquotedblleft{}do\textquotedblright{} that these languages all lean on.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: noun + \ml{ചെയ്യുക} = a new verb}]
This \textquotedblleft{}noun + \emph{ceyyuka}\textquotedblright{} pattern is the twin of Hindi's \textquotedblleft{}noun + \emph{karnā},\textquotedblright{} Tamil's \textquotedblleft{}noun + \emph{sey},\textquotedblright{} Telugu's \textquotedblleft{}noun + \emph{cēyu},\textquotedblright{} and Kannada's \textquotedblleft{}noun + \emph{māḍu}.\textquotedblright{} Five languages, two of them from an unrelated family, all landed on the same trick.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}jōli ceyyuka\textquotedblright{} (to work)
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ñān jōli ceyyunnu}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the Tamil verb that is the \emph{same word} as \emph{ceyyuka} (\emph{sey})
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{saṁsārikkuka}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Malayalam turn \textquotedblleft{}work\textquotedblright{} into \textquotedblleft{}to work,\textquotedblright{} and which Tamil verb is its twin? (\emph{Jōli} + \emph{ceyyuka} = \textquotedblleft{}work-do\textquotedblright{}; Tamil \emph{sey} — the same Dravidian root.)
\end{tcolorbox}

\section[Practice]{Chapter 5 — The first verbs}

\label{lesson:ML-C05-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three verbs, one endlessly simple engine.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — build the sentences}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I speak Malayalam\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ñān malayāḷaṁ saṁsārikkunnu}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I live in Kochi\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ñān kocciyil tāmasikkunnu}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}I work\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ñān jōli ceyyunnu}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}he speaks\textquotedblright{} — \emph{avan saṁsārikkunnu} (the very same verb!)
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — the engine}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the present ending on every verb (\emph{-unnu})
  \item the one thing Malayalam verbs do NOT do (change for person)
  \item what that forces you to always keep (the pronoun \emph{ñān} etc.)
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{saṁsārikkuka} \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{} (Sanskrit-derived; native twin \emph{paṟayuka})
  \item \emph{tāmasikkuka} \textquotedblleft{}to live\textquotedblright{} (Sanskrit-derived; where Tamil uses native \emph{vāḻ})
  \item \emph{ceyyuka} \textquotedblleft{}to do\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \emph{jōli ceyyuka} \textquotedblleft{}to work\textquotedblright{} — the \emph{same root} as Tamil \emph{sey}
  \item \emph{malayāḷaṁ} = \emph{mala} \textquotedblleft{}mountain\textquotedblright{} + \emph{āḷaṁ} \textquotedblleft{}place\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}the mountain land\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Script check — the letters of this chapter}
Cover the romanizations. Find each letter once in the Malayalam above, then say the word it sits in.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഞാൻ}} — \textbf{\ml{ഞ}} \emph{ña}, \textbf{\ml{ൻ}} \emph{n}
  \item \textbf{\ml{പോയി}} — \textbf{\ml{യ}} \emph{ya}
  \item \textbf{\ml{കൊച്ചിയിൽ}} — \textbf{\ml{◌ൊ}} \emph{o}, \textbf{\ml{ച}} \emph{ca}, \textbf{\ml{ൽ}} \emph{l}
  \item \textbf{\ml{സഹായം}} — \textbf{\ml{ഹ}} \emph{ha}
  \item \textbf{\ml{ജോലി}} — \textbf{\ml{ജ}} \emph{ja}, \textbf{\ml{ല}} \emph{la}
\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at each letter, then find it in the word beside it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
In one breath, say your language, your city, and your work in Malayalam — and note what stays the same in every verb. (\emph{Ñān malayāḷaṁ saṁsārikkunnu. Ñān … il tāmasikkunnu. Ñān jōli ceyyunnu} — the verb never changes for person.)
\end{tcolorbox}
